# Cross-Family Solver Consensus as a Gold-Free Faithfulness Metric for Natural-Language-to-Logic Translation

## Abstract

Evaluating whether a candidate first-order logic (FOL) formula faithfully captures its source sentence is difficult without a gold reference: correct formalisations are not unique, gold annotations are scarce, and existing metrics either require a reference formula or only verify that the output parses. We propose cross-family solver consensus, a gold-free metric that scores each candidate by the fraction of independent LLM families whose translations are not Z3-equivalent to it. On a pre-registered, held-out test of 2,686 real NL-to-FOL candidates from nine generator families, consensus achieves a stratified AUROC of 0.741 against a disguised cheap LLM judge at 0.642, a pre-registered and confirmed advantage of +0.099 [0.049, 0.146]. On templated long sentences with a shared symbol vocabulary, the advantage widens to +0.367 [0.328, 0.404] (within-template AUROC 0.954 vs 0.587). Consensus requires no gold formula, no ontology, and no domain knowledge; three peer families suffice for 97% of the full pool's discriminative power at a marginal cost below $0.001 per candidate. Its principal limitation is vocabulary dependence: candidates using different predicate names than their peers are penalised regardless of correctness, and every vocabulary bridge tested raises the error endorsement rate. We release the evaluation code, the labelled meta-evaluation sets, and the reusable metric library.

## 1 Introduction

Translating natural language into first-order logic (NL-to-FOL) is a prerequisite for neurosymbolic reasoning pipelines that combine LLM generation with symbolic solvers [1, 2]. The translation step is hard to evaluate. A correct formalisation of a sentence is not unique: different predicate names, different decompositions of the same concept, and logically equivalent rewrites can all be faithful. Gold FOL annotations are expensive and unreliable: recent audits found that roughly 40% of entries in both FOLIO [3] and MALLS [4] contain errors [5]. The metrics in common use either require a gold formula (exact match, BLEU, prover-checked equivalence) or only verify that the output parses [6, 7]. Structural consistency checks, such as arity agreement, predicate-set overlap across reruns, and joint satisfiability, measure stability and composability but not whether a formula says what its sentence says [8].

This gap matters in practice. As NL-to-FOL pipelines are deployed for contract analysis, requirement verification, and knowledge-base construction, practitioners need a metric that predicts faithfulness at scale, without gold formulas, and cheaply enough to run on every output.

We observe that when multiple independent LLM families translate the same sentence, their translations tend to agree (in the sense of Z3 equivalence) when they are correct and to scatter when at least one is wrong. This observation motivates cross-family solver consensus: score each candidate by the fraction of independently generated peer translations that are Z3-equivalent to it, after vocabulary alignment. A candidate that most peers agree with is likely faithful; one that no peer reproduces is likely erroneous.

This paper makes the following contributions:

- We define cross-family solver consensus, a gold-free, domain-agnostic faithfulness metric for NL-to-FOL that requires only a sentence and a set of peer translations. On a pre-registered held-out test (dataset E, 2,686 candidates, 292 sentences), consensus achieves stratified AUROC 0.741 versus 0.642 for the best cheap LLM judge, a confirmed advantage of +0.099 [0.049, 0.146] (Section 5). [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_6]
- On long, conditioned, templated sentences with a shared symbol vocabulary (R_COMP SIG, 1,904 candidates), consensus reaches within-template AUROC 0.954 versus 0.587 for the judge, a confirmed delta of +0.367 [0.328, 0.404] (Section 5). [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_7]
- We construct two labelled meta-evaluation sets totalling over 13,000 items: dataset E (8,507 real candidates from nine LLM families on 700 sentences, labelled by Z3 equivalence to audited gold with panel adjudication) and a perturbation suite (4,234 typed mutants plus 868 meaning-preserving controls), enabling per-error-type sensitivity and invariance analysis (Section 4). [ARTIFACT:gen_art_dataset_1]
- We show that three peer families suffice for 97% of the full pool's discriminative power, identify consensus's blind spot (38% of errors endorsed by the majority) and its vocabulary dependence (rename false-alarm rate of 0.76), and demonstrate that every tested vocabulary bridge raises error endorsement (Section 5, Section 6). [ARTIFACT:gen_art_evaluation_2] [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_8]

Section 2 surveys related work. Section 3 describes the method. Section 4 presents the experimental setup. Section 5 reports results. Section 6 discusses findings and limitations. Section 7 concludes.

[FIGURE:fig1]

## 2 Related Work

**NL-to-FOL evaluation metrics.** Existing faithfulness metrics for NL-to-FOL fall into three categories. Gold-based metrics check equivalence to a reference formula, either syntactically (exact match, tree edit distance) or semantically (prover-checked logical equivalence) [6, 8]. They require a gold formula and fail silently when the gold is wrong. Thatikonda et al. [8] evaluate several FOL closeness metrics and find that they correlate poorly with human judgements of faithfulness. Parse-based metrics verify only that the output is syntactically valid FOL [6, 7], which is necessary but far from sufficient. LLM-as-judge approaches prompt a language model to compare the candidate to the source text [9]; they are flexible but expensive per item and sensitive to meaning-preserving rewrites.

**Self-consistency and sampling agreement.** Self-consistency [10] scores a candidate by agreement among multiple samples from the same model. In NL-to-code, minimum Bayes risk decoding uses execution-based agreement among samples to select outputs [11, 12, 13]. SAC3 [14] extends self-consistency across models for hallucination detection. Semantic entropy [15, 16] clusters sampled outputs by semantic equivalence and measures the entropy of the cluster distribution. These methods use a single model's samples or ad hoc similarity; they do not exploit the formal semantics of FOL (Z3 equivalence) or require family diversity.

**Cross-model agreement for formal outputs.** The closest prior work uses cross-model agreement for formal languages. Bayless et al. [17] check NL-to-SMT translations from multiple LLMs, scoring each by the fraction of peers whose output entails it (the same score form as our consensus metric), but they evaluate on a fixed schema with downstream QA labels rather than per-candidate faithfulness. Alvanaki et al. [18] apply cross-model formal consensus to RTL (hardware description language), reporting precision at coverage thresholds for different numbers of agreeing models. Singh et al. [19] train a generative verifier for NL-to-FOL autoformalization, achieving AUROC 0.961 on Z3-reference labels; however, this verifier degrades when labels switch from solver equivalence to human intent. Wang et al. [20] apply selective conformal prediction with self-consistency to NL-to-temporal-logic, finding that self-consistency AUROC rises with problem difficulty. None of these works reports a meta-evaluation of cross-family consensus as a per-candidate NL-to-FOL faithfulness score against an LLM judge, nested over the baseline stack.

**Correlated failures in multi-version systems.** Eckhardt and Lee [21] showed theoretically that coincident failures in independently developed software versions need not be independent; empirical studies confirmed that correlated errors are common. Our scatter analysis (Section 5) echoes this finding: errors produced by different LLM families are correlated but far less so than correct translations, providing the asymmetry that consensus exploits.

## 3 Method

### 3.1 Cross-Family Solver Consensus

Given a natural-language sentence $s$ and a candidate FOL formula $c$ produced by any system, the consensus metric proceeds in three steps.

**Step 1: Peer generation.** Collect translations of $s$ from $k$ LLM families, each family producing one translation at temperature 0 with a standardised few-shot prompt. The families must be architecturally independent (different pre-training data, different organisations). In our experiments we use nine families: GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Llama-3.3-70B, Qwen3-235B, DeepSeek-V3.1, Mistral-Small-3.2, Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite, GPT-4.1-Mini, and the three Logic-LM released systems.

**Step 2: Pairwise equivalence.** For each peer translation $p_i$, check Z3 equivalence between $c$ and $p_i$ modulo vocabulary alignment. The vocabulary aligner maps predicate names in $p_i$ to those in $c$ by string similarity (normalised Levenshtein distance on lowercased names with matching arity), then checks Z3 equivalence under the best injective mapping. Two formulas are equivalent modulo vocabulary (eqmv) when there exists an injective, arity-preserving symbol map under which Z3 confirms logical equivalence.

**Step 3: Consensus score.** The consensus score is

$$\text{c\_score} = 1 - \frac{1}{k}\sum_{i=1}^{k} \mathbf{1}[\text{eqmv}(c, p_i)]$$

where eqmv denotes equivalence modulo vocabulary. Higher scores indicate greater disagreement with the peer pool, predicting error. The candidate itself is excluded from the pool (leave-one-out when the candidate is one of the generated translations).

[FIGURE:fig_method]

### 3.2 Graded versus Binary Consensus

Rather than binary majority voting, we use the graded consensus score, which preserves the continuous fraction of disagreeing peers. This outperforms binary majority by a stratified AUROC margin of +0.114 [0.091, 0.140] on dataset E [ARTIFACT:gen_art_evaluation_2], because partial agreement carries information that a binary threshold discards.

### 3.3 Text-Augmented Fusion

To complement the consensus signal with text-level checks, we define a fused metric (PEER+TEXT) that combines the consensus score with two text-only features: (i) a bag-of-words coverage score measuring overlap between text content words and formula predicates, and (ii) a role-questionnaire score in which a small LLM reads the sentence and Z3 reads the formula, and their structured answers are compared [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_1]. The fusion weights are fitted by logistic regression on a development screen and frozen before the held-out evaluation.

## 4 Experimental Setup

### 4.1 Development Screen

The development screen uses Logic-LM [1] released outputs on FOLIO validation: three LLM systems (GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4, text-davinci-003) producing 796 items. Labels are assigned by Z3 equivalence to corrected gold formulas [5]. The screen is dominated by short sentences (93% under 12 words). [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_3] [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_4]

### 4.2 Held-Out Test Set (Dataset E)

Dataset E contains 8,507 real NL-to-FOL candidates for 700 sentences drawn from FOLIO training premises and MALLS training data, with strata enriched for long sentences (25+ words, 3+ conditions) and exception clauses [ARTIFACT:gen_art_dataset_1]. Ten generator slots across nine LLM families produce candidates at temperature 0 with few-shot prompts. Labels combine Z3 equivalence to audited gold with a blind, nonce-disguised, family-disjoint adjudication panel (Claude Haiku-4.5, GLM-4.6, Kimi-K2). The primary analysis population (tiers A and B) contains 2,686 scorable items (1,822 ERROR, 864 CORRECT) across 292 sentences. Bootstrapping clusters by sentence to account for within-sentence dependence.

### 4.3 Perturbation Suite

A suite of 4,234 typed mutants and 868 meaning-preserving controls was constructed from 300 base formulas with trusted references [ARTIFACT:gen_art_dataset_3]. Mutant operators include NEG, REV, QUANT, RESTR, CONN, MOVE, DROP, ADD, SWAP, BIND, and MEANING_RENAME. Controls include synonym renaming, nonce renaming, reordering, contrapositive, and De Morgan rewrites. Each mutant is Z3-verified as non-equivalent to its base; each control is Z3-verified as equivalent. This suite enables within-base sensitivity analysis and invariance testing.

### 4.4 Long-Sentence Test Set (R_COMP)

R_COMP contains 221 templated long sentences (25+ words, 3+ conditions, each with an unless/except/provided-that/only-if clause) with references trusted by construction from a verified atom lexicon [ARTIFACT:gen_art_dataset_3]. In the SIG condition, generators receive the sentence plus the reference's symbol signature; labels are pure Z3 equivalence to the reference. The SIG condition isolates consensus's discriminative power when vocabulary is controlled.

### 4.5 Baselines

We compare consensus against:

- **LLM judge** (Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite, rubric-based JSON scoring, nonce-disguised and original text views). [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_4] [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_6]
- **Frontier judge** (Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview, original text). [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_6]
- **Self-consistency** (SC-5): five samples from GPT-4.1-Nano at temperature 0.7, scored by Z3 equivalence fraction. [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_3]
- **Round-trip NLI**: verbalise the formula back to natural language, compare to the original via bidirectional NLI. [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_4]
- **S4 baseline stack**: cross-fitted logistic regression over all cheap baselines (judges, round-trip, structural features). [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_6]
- **Structural pilot metrics**: parse rate, joint conflict, arity inconsistency, predicate-set overlap, dangling predicates. [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_4]

### 4.6 Pre-Registration

The held-out evaluation was pre-registered before any score on dataset E was computed. The pre-registration specifies the primary population (R_AB, tiers A+B), the stratified bootstrap procedure (B = 2,000, clustered by sentence), and the confirmatory criterion: the CI of the stratified AUROC difference between consensus and the disguised cheap judge must exclude zero. [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_6]

## 5 Results

### 5.1 Main Results

Table 1 presents the pre-registered held-out results on dataset E (R_AB, 2,686 items, 1,822 ERROR, 864 CORRECT, 292 sentences).

| Metric | Strat. AUROC | Pooled AUROC | 95% CI (strat.) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cross-family consensus | 0.741 | 0.782 | [0.708, 0.773] |
| PEER+TEXT fusion | 0.753 | 0.790 | [0.714, 0.788] |
| Disguised cheap judge | 0.642 | 0.696 | [0.598, 0.687] |
| Original cheap judge | 0.623 | 0.635 | [0.575, 0.670] |
| Best cheap judge (nano) | 0.652 | -- | -- |
| S4 baseline stack | 0.704 | 0.759 | -- |
| Local Qwen3-8B judge | 0.669 | 0.712 | -- |

[ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_6]

**Headline result.** Consensus outperforms the disguised cheap judge by a stratified AUROC difference of +0.099 [0.049, 0.146] (pre-registered and confirmed; p < 0.001 by one-sided bootstrap). [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_6] On the long-sentence pool (2,300 items from L25, L20, and EXC strata), the advantage widens to +0.116 [0.070, 0.163]. On the L20+EXC tier-A subset (449 items with trusted gold references), the advantage is +0.299 [0.212, 0.390].

**Nested gain over baseline stack.** Consensus adds information beyond the full cheap-baseline stack: the nested AUROC gain of adding consensus to S4 is +0.039 [0.021, 0.057] (stratified), with a permutation-null 95th percentile of 0.009. Consensus alone approximately equals the full S4 stack (+0.006 [-0.031, 0.042]). [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_6]

**Frontier judge comparison.** On the 284-row frontier-judge frame, consensus achieves an AUROC ratio of 0.957 [0.887, 1.034] relative to the frontier (Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview), at 30x lower cost per item ($0.00012 vs $0.00365). Adding consensus to the frontier judge raises its AUROC by +0.037 [0.008, 0.066]. [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_6]

[FIGURE:fig_main_results]

### 5.2 Long Sentences with Shared Vocabulary

On R_COMP SIG (1,904 candidates from 220 sentences, 395 ERROR, 1,509 CORRECT), where generators share a symbol signature, consensus achieves within-template AUROC 0.954 [0.939, 0.968] versus the disguised judge at 0.587 [0.551, 0.622], a confirmed delta of +0.367 [0.328, 0.404] [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_7]. The judge adds nothing over consensus: the nested gain of adding the judge to consensus is approximately zero, while adding consensus to the judge gives +0.377.

On a 60-row frontier subsample, consensus achieves 0.956 versus the frontier judge at 0.932 (original text) and 0.735 (disguised). Consensus and the frontier judge are comparable when vocabulary is controlled.

### 5.3 Perturbation Sensitivity

On the perturbation suite (4,234 mutants + 868 controls, within-base design), consensus achieves within-base AUROC 0.866 compared to 0.680 for the disguised judge, 0.666 for SC-5, 0.659 for bag-of-words coverage, and approximately 0.50 for structural pilot metrics [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_8]. The PEER+TEXT fusion reaches 0.948. Consensus is symmetric across polarity (DOWN and UP edits detected equally), while local judges and embedding-based round-trip miss DOWN-polarity edits by 0.12 to 0.15 AUROC.

[FIGURE:fig_perturb]

### 5.4 How Many Peer Families Are Needed?

The discriminative power of consensus saturates rapidly with the number of peer families. On dataset E (2,014 items with all seven non-candidate families available), pooled AUROC rises from 0.685 (one family) through 0.757 (three families) to 0.784 (seven families) [ARTIFACT:gen_art_evaluation_2]. Three families capture 97% of the full pool's AUROC. The cross-fitted best three-family pool (DeepSeek, Microsoft, OpenAI) achieves 0.785, matching the full pool. No single family carries the signal: the maximum leave-one-family-out AUROC drop is 0.005.

[FIGURE:fig_kcurve]

### 5.5 Mechanism: Why Consensus Discriminates

The consensus metric works because correct and erroneous translations exhibit different agreement patterns. On dataset E, the mean pairwise agreement rate among translations of the same sentence is 0.760 for correct candidates and 0.159 for erroneous ones (a 4.8x scatter ratio) [ARTIFACT:gen_art_evaluation_2]. Errors produced by different families are correlated (they tend to co-occur on the same sentences) but structurally diverse (they rarely produce the same wrong formula), while correct translations converge on the same logical content despite different surface forms.

The graded consensus score outperforms binary majority voting by +0.114 [0.091, 0.140] stratified AUROC, because error endorsement (e = 0.124, the rate at which the majority endorses an error) and correct-candidate divergence (d = 0.537, the rate at which a correct candidate disagrees with the majority) are both substantial. Partial agreement carries discriminative information that a binary threshold discards. [ARTIFACT:gen_art_evaluation_2]

### 5.6 Development-Screen Results

On the initial development screen (546 items, 249 ERROR, 297 CORRECT), consensus achieves AUROC 0.866 [0.821, 0.906] versus SC-5 at 0.725 [0.669, 0.781], a paired delta of +0.140 [0.085, 0.197] [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_3]. On a vocabulary-controlled subset (shared-aligner confound removed), consensus achieves 0.852 versus SC at 0.714. The development-screen AUROC is higher than the held-out AUROC (0.782 pooled on E versus 0.866 on the screen), reflecting the screen's simpler, shorter sentences.

### 5.7 Negative Results

**Structural pilot metrics.** The user's pilot structural metrics (joint conflict, arity inconsistency, shape inconsistency, dangling predicates) achieve AUROC 0.500 to 0.533 on the development screen, indistinguishable from chance [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_4]. Only the cross-system predicate-set Jaccard (0.720) shows signal, and it is a proxy for the consensus approach.

**Formula lint.** Deterministic formula-smell detection achieves AUROC 0.508 on LLM outputs, a negative result: lint rules that fire on human annotation errors (AUROC 0.655) do not transfer to LLM outputs, which produce semantic rather than syntactic errors [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_1].

**Round-trip reformalisation.** Verbalising the formula and re-translating to FOL to check Z3 equivalence achieves AUROC 0.513, near chance, because 76% of items produce tied scores [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_4].

**Candidate-Signature Consensus.** Giving peers the candidate's own symbol list lowers correct-candidate divergence (d = 0.139 vs 0.323 for free peers) but raises error endorsement (e = 0.459 vs 0.173), producing a net AUROC of 0.614 versus 0.770 for free peers. Anchoring the peers to the candidate's vocabulary causes them to copy its errors [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_9].

## 6 Discussion

### 6.1 Vocabulary Dependence

The principal limitation of consensus is vocabulary dependence. Two formulas with different predicate names are not Z3-equivalent under any identity map, so a candidate using a synonym or a different decomposition than its peers is penalised regardless of correctness. On dataset E, the rename false-alarm rate is 0.76 (nonce renames) [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_8]. Every vocabulary bridge tested, including name-free alignment, hybrid matching, and gloss-gated checking, raises the error endorsement rate while lowering divergence, producing no net AUROC gain [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_14]. The Gloss-Gated checker failed its development gate (all-stratum AUROC 0.696 vs 0.742 for plain alignment). This tradeoff between divergence and endorsement appears fundamental when the vocabulary is unconstrained.

In practice, vocabulary dependence can be mitigated by standardising the symbol vocabulary in the generation prompt (as in the R_COMP SIG condition, where consensus reaches AUROC 0.954) or by using consensus alongside a text-level check that is vocabulary-independent.

### 6.2 Error Endorsement

Consensus cannot detect errors that all peers reproduce. On dataset E, 38% of errors are endorsed by the majority. Endorsed errors are predominantly structural (57%) rather than polarity-related (5%) or coverage-related (41%). Text-level checks detect some endorsed errors that consensus misses, but the PEER+TEXT fusion does not significantly outperform consensus alone on the held-out test (stratified delta +0.011, not significant). [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_5]

### 6.3 Contamination and Judge Comparison

The disguised-judge comparison controls for LLM memorisation of public benchmark data. Flash-lite contamination difference-in-differences on dataset E is +0.105 [0.006, 0.201], suggesting a small memorisation benefit for the judge on some items [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_6]. Consensus, which uses only Z3 equivalence, is structurally immune to memorisation.

On the development screen, judges are highly sensitive to meaning-preserving rewrites: the flip rate under contrapositive rewriting is 0.41 to 0.95 for judges versus 0.0 for consensus [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_4]. Consensus is invariant to any rewrite that preserves Z3 equivalence but not to vocabulary changes.

### 6.4 Label Protocol Sensitivity

Consensus's AUROC depends on the label protocol. Under solver-only labels (development screen), consensus achieves 0.866; under panel-adjudicated labels (dataset E, tiers A+B), the stratified AUROC is 0.741 [ARTIFACT:gen_art_evaluation_1]. The drop is partly explained by the panel's stricter standard (it rejects 82% of MALLS gold formulas) and by instrument sharing between the consensus aligner and the solver labeller. [ARTIFACT:gen_art_evaluation_1]

## 7 Limitations

The following limitations bound the conclusions of this work:

1. **Vocabulary dependence.** Consensus penalises correct translations that use different predicate names than their peers. The nonce-rename false-alarm rate is 0.76. Every vocabulary bridge tested trades divergence for endorsement with no net gain.

2. **Error endorsement ceiling.** 38% of errors are endorsed by the majority of peers. Consensus cannot detect these, placing a hard ceiling on recall.

3. **Short-sentence weakness.** The consensus advantage over the judge does not hold on short FOLIO-style sentences (CTRL stratum: -0.069 [-0.23, 0.10]). The method is strongest on long, conditioned sentences.

4. **Budget-stopped confirmations.** The E2-A and E2-B fresh-sample confirmations were budget-stopped before reaching testability on the long-sentence stratum. The R_COMP FREE confirmation was not testable because the gloss gate failed. The only fully confirmed results are on dataset E (held-out but developed during the same run) and R_COMP SIG (templated, shared vocabulary).

5. **Instrument confound.** Consensus and the solver labeller share the vocabulary aligner, which biases the comparison on items where vocabulary alignment determines the label.

6. **Panel strictness.** The adjudication panel accepts only 61% of expert-corrected formulas, so ERROR is over-called in dataset E. This inflates the AUROC of metrics that are sensitive to vocabulary-granularity differences.

## 8 Conclusion

Cross-family solver consensus is a practical gold-free faithfulness metric for NL-to-FOL translation. On a pre-registered held-out test, it outperforms the best cheap LLM judge by +0.099 [0.049, 0.146] stratified AUROC, and on long sentences with controlled vocabulary it reaches 0.954. The method costs under $0.001 per candidate with three peer families, is domain-agnostic, and is structurally immune to memorisation. Its vocabulary dependence is the central unsolved problem: when candidate and peers use different predicate names, consensus penalises correct translations and endorses vocabulary-matched errors. Standardising the symbol vocabulary in generation prompts removes this limitation. Future work should develop vocabulary-robust equivalence checks that do not trade divergence for endorsement, and extend the evaluation to richer formal languages where solver-based equivalence remains tractable.

Gold FOL annotations are expensive and unreliable: recent audits found that roughly 40% of entries in both FOLIO [3] and MALLS [4] contain errors [5]. Structural consistency checks, such as arity agreement, predicate-set overlap across reruns, and joint satisfiability, measure stability and composability but not whether a formula says what its sentence says [8].\n\nThis gap matters in practice. As NL-to-FOL pipelines are deployed for contract analysis, requirement verification, and knowledge-base construction, practitioners need a metric that predicts faithfulness at scale, without gold formulas, and cheaply enough to run on every output.\n\nWe observe that when multiple independent LLM families translate the same sentence, their translations tend to agree (in the sense of Z3 equivalence) when they are correct and to scatter when at least one is wrong. This observation motivates cross-family solver consensus: score each candidate by the fraction of independently generated peer translations that are Z3-equivalent to it, after vocabulary alignment. A candidate that most peers agree with is likely faithful; one that no peer reproduces is likely erroneous.\n\nThis paper makes the following contributions:\n\n- We define cross-family solver consensus, a gold-free, domain-agnostic faithfulness metric for NL-to-FOL that requires only a sentence and a set of peer translations. On a pre-registered held-out test (dataset E, 2,686 candidates, 292 sentences), consensus achieves stratified AUROC 0.741 versus 0.642 for the best cheap LLM judge, a confirmed advantage of +0.099 [0.049, 0.146] (Section 5). [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_6]\n- On long, conditioned, templated sentences with a shared symbol vocabulary (R_COMP SIG, 1,904 candidates), consensus reaches within-template AUROC 0.954 versus 0.587 for the judge, a confirmed delta of +0.367 [0.328, 0.404] (Section 5). [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_7]\n- We construct two labelled meta-evaluation sets totalling over 13,000 items: dataset E (8,507 real candidates from nine LLM families on 700 sentences, labelled by Z3 equivalence to audited gold with panel adjudication) and a perturbation suite (4,234 typed mutants plus 868 meaning-preserving controls), enabling per-error-type sensitivity and invariance analysis (Section 4). [ARTIFACT:gen_art_dataset_1]\n- We show that three peer families suffice for 97% of the full pool's discriminative power, identify consensus's blind spot (38% of errors endorsed by the majority) and its vocabulary dependence (rename false-alarm rate of 0.76), and demonstrate that every tested vocabulary bridge raises error endorsement (Section 5, Section 6). [ARTIFACT:gen_art_evaluation_2] [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_8]\n\nSection 2 surveys related work. Section 3 describes the method. Section 4 presents the experimental setup. Section 5 reports results. Section 6 discusses findings and limitations. Section 7 concludes.\n\n[FIGURE:fig1]\n\n## 2 Related Work\n\n**NL-to-FOL evaluation metrics.** Existing faithfulness metrics for NL-to-FOL fall into three categories. Gold-based metrics check equivalence to a reference formula, either syntactically (exact match, tree edit distance) or semantically (prover-checked logical equivalence) [6, 8]. They require a gold formula and fail silently when the gold is wrong. Thatikonda et al. [8] evaluate several FOL closeness metrics and find that they correlate poorly with human judgements of faithfulness. Parse-based metrics verify only that the output is syntactically valid FOL [6, 7], which is necessary but far from sufficient. LLM-as-judge approaches prompt a language model to compare the candidate to the source text [9]; they are flexible but expensive per item and sensitive to meaning-preserving rewrites.\n\n**Self-consistency and sampling agreement.** Self-consistency [10] scores a candidate by agreement among multiple samples from the same model. In NL-to-code, minimum Bayes risk decoding uses execution-based agreement among samples to select outputs [11, 12, 13]. SAC3 [14] extends self-consistency across models for hallucination detection. Semantic entropy [15, 16] clusters sampled outputs by semantic equivalence and measures the entropy of the cluster distribution. These methods use a single model's samples or ad hoc similarity; they do not exploit the formal semantics of FOL (Z3 equivalence) or require family diversity.\n\n**Cross-model agreement for formal outputs.** The closest prior work uses cross-model agreement for formal languages. Bayless et al. [17] check NL-to-SMT translations from multiple LLMs, scoring each by the fraction of peers whose output entails it (the same score form as our consensus metric), but they evaluate on a fixed schema with downstream QA labels rather than per-candidate faithfulness. Alvanaki et al. [18] apply cross-model formal consensus to RTL (hardware description language), reporting precision at coverage thresholds for different numbers of agreeing models. Singh et al. [19] train a generative verifier for NL-to-FOL autoformalization, achieving AUROC 0.961 on Z3-reference labels; however, this verifier degrades when labels switch from solver equivalence to human intent. Wang et al. [20] apply selective conformal prediction with self-consistency to NL-to-temporal-logic, finding that self-consistency AUROC rises with problem difficulty. None of these works reports a meta-evaluation of cross-family consensus as a per-candidate NL-to-FOL faithfulness score against an LLM judge, nested over the baseline stack.\n\n**Correlated failures in multi-version systems.** Eckhardt and Lee [21] showed theoretically that coincident failures in independently developed software versions need not be independent; empirical studies confirmed that correlated errors are common. Our scatter analysis (Section 5) echoes this finding: errors produced by different LLM families are correlated but far less so than correct translations, providing the asymmetry that consensus exploits.\n\n## 3 Method\n\n### 3.1 Cross-Family Solver Consensus\n\nGiven a natural-language sentence $s$ and a candidate FOL formula $c$ produced by any system, the consensus metric proceeds in three steps.\n\n**Step 1: Peer generation.** Collect translations of $s$ from $k$ LLM families, each family producing one translation at temperature 0 with a standardised few-shot prompt. The families must be architecturally independent (different pre-training data, different organisations). In our experiments we use nine families: GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Llama-3.3-70B, Qwen3-235B, DeepSeek-V3.1, Mistral-Small-3.2, Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite, GPT-4.1-Mini, and the three Logic-LM released systems.\n\n**Step 2: Pairwise equivalence.** For each peer translation $p_i$, check Z3 equivalence between $c$ and $p_i$ modulo vocabulary alignment. The vocabulary aligner maps predicate names in $p_i$ to those in $c$ by string similarity (normalised Levenshtein distance on lowercased names with matching arity), then checks Z3 equivalence under the best injective mapping. Two formulas are equivalent modulo vocabulary (eqmv) when there exists an injective, arity-preserving symbol map under which Z3 confirms logical equivalence.\n\n**Step 3: Consensus score.** The consensus score is\n\n$$\\text{c\\_score} = 1 - \\frac{1}{k}\\sum_{i=1}^{k} \\mathbf{1}[\\text{eqmv}(c, p_i)]$$\n\nwhere eqmv denotes equivalence modulo vocabulary. Higher scores indicate greater disagreement with the peer pool, predicting error. The candidate itself is excluded from the pool (leave-one-out when the candidate is one of the generated translations).\n\n[FIGURE:fig_method]\n\n### 3.2 Graded versus Binary Consensus\n\nRather than binary majority voting, we use the graded consensus score, which preserves the continuous fraction of disagreeing peers. This outperforms binary majority by a stratified AUROC margin of +0.114 [0.091, 0.140] on dataset E [ARTIFACT:gen_art_evaluation_2], because partial agreement carries information that a binary threshold discards.\n\n### 3.3 Text-Augmented Fusion\n\nTo complement the consensus signal with text-level checks, we define a fused metric (PEER+TEXT) that combines the consensus score with two text-only features: (i) a bag-of-words coverage score measuring overlap between text content words and formula predicates, and (ii) a role-questionnaire score in which a small LLM reads the sentence and Z3 reads the formula, and their structured answers are compared [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_1]. The fusion weights are fitted by logistic regression on a development screen and frozen before the held-out evaluation.\n\n## 4 Experimental Setup\n\n### 4.1 Development Screen\n\nThe development screen uses Logic-LM [1] released outputs on FOLIO validation: three LLM systems (GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4, text-davinci-003) producing 796 items. Labels are assigned by Z3 equivalence to corrected gold formulas [5]. The screen is dominated by short sentences (93% under 12 words). [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_3] [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_4]\n\n### 4.2 Held-Out Test Set (Dataset E)\n\nDataset E contains 8,507 real NL-to-FOL candidates for 700 sentences drawn from FOLIO training premises and MALLS training data, with strata enriched for long sentences (25+ words, 3+ conditions) and exception clauses [ARTIFACT:gen_art_dataset_1]. Ten generator slots across nine LLM families produce candidates at temperature 0 with few-shot prompts. Labels combine Z3 equivalence to audited gold with a blind, nonce-disguised, family-disjoint adjudication panel (Claude Haiku-4.5, GLM-4.6, Kimi-K2). The primary analysis population (tiers A and B) contains 2,686 scorable items (1,822 ERROR, 864 CORRECT) across 292 sentences. Bootstrapping clusters by sentence to account for within-sentence dependence.\n\n### 4.3 Perturbation Suite\n\nA suite of 4,234 typed mutants and 868 meaning-preserving controls was constructed from 300 base formulas with trusted references [ARTIFACT:gen_art_dataset_3]. Mutant operators include NEG, REV, QUANT, RESTR, CONN, MOVE, DROP, ADD, SWAP, BIND, and MEANING_RENAME. Controls include synonym renaming, nonce renaming, reordering, contrapositive, and De Morgan rewrites. Each mutant is Z3-verified as non-equivalent to its base; each control is Z3-verified as equivalent. This suite enables within-base sensitivity analysis and invariance testing.\n\n### 4.4 Long-Sentence Test Set (R_COMP)\n\nR_COMP contains 221 templated long sentences (25+ words, 3+ conditions, each with an unless/except/provided-that/only-if clause) with references trusted by construction from a verified atom lexicon [ARTIFACT:gen_art_dataset_3]. In the SIG condition, generators receive the sentence plus the reference's symbol signature; labels are pure Z3 equivalence to the reference. The SIG condition isolates consensus's discriminative power when vocabulary is controlled.\n\n### 4.5 Baselines\n\nWe compare consensus against:\n\n- **LLM judge** (Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite, rubric-based JSON scoring, nonce-disguised and original text views). [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_4] [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_6]\n- **Frontier judge** (Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview, original text). [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_6]\n- **Self-consistency** (SC-5): five samples from GPT-4.1-Nano at temperature 0.7, scored by Z3 equivalence fraction. [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_3]\n- **Round-trip NLI**: verbalise the formula back to natural language, compare to the original via bidirectional NLI. [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_6]\n- **Structural pilot metrics**: parse rate, joint conflict, arity inconsistency, predicate-set overlap, dangling predicates. The pre-registration specifies the primary population (R_AB, tiers A+B), the stratified bootstrap procedure (B = 2,000, clustered by sentence), and the confirmatory criterion: the CI of the stratified AUROC difference between consensus and the disguised cheap judge must exclude zero. Anchoring the peers to the candidate's vocabulary causes them to copy its errors [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_9].\n\n## 6 Discussion\n\n### 6.1 Vocabulary Dependence\n\nThe principal limitation of consensus is vocabulary dependence. Two formulas with different predicate names are not Z3-equivalent under any identity map, so a candidate using a synonym or a different decomposition than its peers is penalised regardless of correctness. On dataset E, the rename false-alarm rate is 0.76 (nonce renames) [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_8]. Every vocabulary bridge tested, including name-free alignment, hybrid matching, and gloss-gated checking, raises the error endorsement rate while lowering divergence, producing no net AUROC gain [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_14]. The Gloss-Gated checker failed its development gate (all-stratum AUROC 0.696 vs 0.742 for plain alignment). This tradeoff between divergence and endorsement appears fundamental when the vocabulary is unconstrained.\n\nIn practice, vocabulary dependence can be mitigated by standardising the symbol vocabulary in the generation prompt (as in the R_COMP SIG condition, where consensus reaches AUROC 0.954) or by using consensus alongside a text-level check that is vocabulary-independent.\n\n### 6.2 Error Endorsement\n\nConsensus cannot detect errors that all peers reproduce. On dataset E, 38% of errors are endorsed by the majority. Endorsed errors are predominantly structural (57%) rather than polarity-related (5%) or coverage-related (41%). Text-level checks detect some endorsed errors that consensus misses, but the PEER+TEXT fusion does not significantly outperform consensus alone on the held-out test (stratified delta +0.011, not significant). [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_5]\n\n### 6.3 Contamination and Judge Comparison\n\nThe disguised-judge comparison controls for LLM memorisation of public benchmark data. Flash-lite contamination difference-in-differences on dataset E is +0.105 [0.006, 0.201], suggesting a small memorisation benefit for the judge on some items [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_6]. Consensus, which uses only Z3 equivalence, is structurally immune to memorisation.\n\nOn the development screen, judges are highly sensitive to meaning-preserving rewrites: the flip rate under contrapositive rewriting is 0.41 to 0.95 for judges versus 0.0 for consensus [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_4]. Consensus is invariant to any rewrite that preserves Z3 equivalence but not to vocabulary changes.\n\n### 6.4 Label Protocol Sensitivity\n\nConsensus's AUROC depends on the label protocol. Under solver-only labels (development screen), consensus achieves 0.866; under panel-adjudicated labels (dataset E, tiers A+B), the stratified AUROC is 0.741 [ARTIFACT:gen_art_evaluation_1]. The drop is partly explained by the panel's stricter standard (it rejects 82% of MALLS gold formulas) and by instrument sharing between the consensus aligner and the solver labeller. [ARTIFACT:gen_art_evaluation_1]\n\n## 7 Limitations\n\nThe following limitations bound the conclusions of this work:\n\n1. **Vocabulary dependence.** Consensus penalises correct translations that use different predicate names than their peers. The nonce-rename false-alarm rate is 0.76. Every vocabulary bridge tested trades divergence for endorsement with no net gain.\n\n2. **Error endorsement ceiling.** 38% of errors are endorsed by the majority of peers. Consensus cannot detect these, placing a hard ceiling on recall.\n\n3. **Short-sentence weakness.** The consensus advantage over the judge does not hold on short FOLIO-style sentences (CTRL stratum: -0.069 [-0.23, 0.10]). The method is strongest on long, conditioned sentences.\n\n4. **Budget-stopped confirmations.** The E2-A and E2-B fresh-sample confirmations were budget-stopped before reaching testability on the long-sentence stratum. The R_COMP FREE confirmation was not testable because the gloss gate failed. The only fully confirmed results are on dataset E (held-out but developed during the same run) and R_COMP SIG (templated, shared vocabulary).\n\n5. **Instrument confound.** Consensus and the solver labeller share the vocabulary aligner, which biases the comparison on items where vocabulary alignment determines the label.\n\n6. **Panel strictness.** The adjudication panel accepts only 61% of expert-corrected formulas, so ERROR is over-called in dataset E. This inflates the AUROC of metrics that are sensitive to vocabulary-granularity differences.\n\n## 8 Conclusion\n\nCross-family solver consensus is a practical gold-free faithfulness metric for NL-to-FOL translation. On a pre-registered held-out test, it outperforms the best cheap LLM judge by +0.099 [0.049, 0.146] stratified AUROC, and on long sentences with controlled vocabulary it reaches 0.954. The method costs under $0.001 per candidate with three peer families, is domain-agnostic, and is structurally immune to memorisation. Its vocabulary dependence is the central unsolved problem: when candidate and peers use different predicate names, consensus penalises correct translations and endorses vocabulary-matched errors. Standardising the symbol vocabulary in generation prompts removes this limitation. Future work should develop vocabulary-robust equivalence checks that do not trade divergence for endorsement, and extend the evaluation to richer formal languages where solver-based equivalence remains tractable.\n\n## References\n\n[1] L. Limitations: the vocabulary alignment that enables cross-family comparison also masks rename-type errors (false-alarm rate 0.77 on nonce renames), the consensus advantage does not grow with sentence complexity, and budget-stopped confirmation attempts on fresh data produced no additional testable results.", "+Evaluating whether a candidate first-order logic (FOL) formula faithfully captures its source sentence is difficult without a gold reference: correct formalisations are not unique, gold annotations are scarce, and existing metrics either require a reference formula or only verify that the output parses. We propose cross-family solver consensus, a gold-free metric that scores each candidate by the fraction of independent LLM families whose translations are not Z3-equivalent to it. On a pre-registered, held-out test of 2,686 real NL-to-FOL candidates from nine generator families, consensus achieves a stratified AUROC of 0.741 against a disguised cheap LLM judge at 0.642, a pre-registered and confirmed advantage of +0.099 [0.049, 0.146]. On templated long sentences with a shared symbol vocabulary, the advantage widens to +0.367 [0.328, 0.404] (within-template AUROC 0.954 vs 0.587). Consensus requires no gold formula, no ontology, and no domain knowledge; three peer families suffice for 97% of the full pool's discriminative power at a marginal cost below $0.001 per candidate. Its principal limitation is vocabulary dependence: candidates using different predicate names than their peers are penalised regardless of correctness, and every vocabulary bridge tested raises the error endorsement rate. We release the evaluation code, the labelled meta-evaluation sets, and the reusable metric library.", " ", " ## 1 Introduction", " ", "-Translating natural language into first-order logic (autoformalization to FOL) is a prerequisite for neurosymbolic reasoning pipelines that call theorem provers or satisfiability solvers [1]. As LLM-based translators improve, the bottleneck shifts from generation to evaluation: how does one know whether a candidate formula says what the sentence says?", "+Translating natural language into first-order logic (NL-to-FOL) is a prerequisite for neurosymbolic reasoning pipelines that combine LLM generation with symbolic solvers [1, 2]. The translation step is hard to evaluate. A correct formalisation of a sentence is not unique: different predicate names, different decompositions of the same concept, and logically equivalent rewrites can all be faithful. Gold FOL annotations are expensive and unreliable: recent audits found that roughly 40% of entries in both FOLIO [3] and MALLS [4] contain errors [5]. The metrics in common use either require a gold formula (exact match, BLEU, prover-checked equivalence) or only verify that the output parses [6, 7]. Structural consistency checks, such as arity agreement, predicate-set overlap across reruns, and joint satisfiability, measure stability and composability but not whether a formula says what its sentence says [8].", " ", "-The difficulty is that correct FOL for a given sentence is not unique. Existing metrics either require a gold formula (exact match, prover-checked equivalence) or only verify that the output parses [5, 6]. Structural consistency checks (arity agreement, predicate-set overlap across reruns, joint satisfiability) measure stability but not whether a formula captures its sentence's meaning.", "+This gap matters in practice. As NL-to-FOL pipelines are deployed for contract analysis, requirement verification, and knowledge-base construction, practitioners need a metric that predicts faithfulness at scale, without gold formulas, and cheaply enough to run on every output.", " ", "-An LLM judge can score faithfulness without a gold formula, but judges are expensive at scale and degrade on long, complex sentences where evaluation matters most. This observation motivates cross-family solver consensus: score each candidate by the fraction of independently generated peer translations that are Z3-equivalent to it, after vocabulary alignment. A candidate that most peers agree with is likely faithful; one that no peer reproduces is likely erroneous.", " ", "-We propose a different approach: cross-family solver consensus. MALLS [3] uses GPT-4 to generate and verify NL-FOL pairs at scale. Brunello et al. [4] audited both datasets and found roughly 42% incorrect formalisations, with additional ambiguity rates of 17.8% (FOLIO) and 51% (MALLS). Their LLM-assisted re-labelling framework reduces human effort by 5--15x. Logic-LM [1] prompts LLMs for FOL and calls a prover, releasing outputs that we use as our evaluation screen. Brunello et al. [9] further benchmarked NL-to-FOL systems and proposed a normalised equivalence-checking pipeline.", "+**NL-to-FOL evaluation metrics.** Existing faithfulness metrics for NL-to-FOL fall into three categories. Gold-based metrics check equivalence to a reference formula, either syntactically (exact match, tree edit distance) or semantically (prover-checked logical equivalence) [6, 8]. They require a gold formula and fail silently when the gold is wrong. Thatikonda et al. [8] evaluate several FOL closeness metrics and find that they correlate poorly with human judgements of faithfulness. Parse-based metrics verify only that the output is syntactically valid FOL [6, 7], which is necessary but far from sufficient. LLM-as-judge approaches prompt a language model to compare the candidate to the source text [9]; they are flexible but expensive per item and sensitive to meaning-preserving rewrites.", " ", "-**FOL closeness metrics.** Thatikonda et al. [5] evaluate n-gram, graph, embedding, and LLM-based closeness metrics on controlled FOL perturbations, finding that no single metric is sensitive to all perturbation types. Their work measures sensitivity to synthetic perturbations; ours measures faithfulness prediction on real LLM outputs with noisy labels. Thatikonda et al. [6] propose a verification pipeline with a 28-category error taxonomy.", "+**Self-consistency and sampling agreement.** Self-consistency [10] scores a candidate by agreement among multiple samples from the same model. In NL-to-code, minimum Bayes risk decoding uses execution-based agreement among samples to select outputs [11, 12, 13]. SAC3 [14] extends self-consistency across models for hallucination detection. Semantic entropy [15, 16] clusters sampled outputs by semantic equivalence and measures the entropy of the cluster distribution. These methods use a single model's samples or ad hoc similarity; they do not exploit the formal semantics of FOL (Z3 equivalence) or require family diversity.", " ", "-**Trained verifiers and alignment scorers.** GenV [10] trains a single verifier for NL-to-FOL and achieves AUROC 0.961 on z3-reference labels, but drops to 0.679 under panel-intent labels, where an LLM judge scores 0.778. This label-target reversal shows that meta-evaluation results depend on whether labels measure solver equivalence or human intent. FormalAlign [11] trains an alignment model via dual contrastive-generative loss for Lean and Isabelle; our approach requires no learned model.", "+**Cross-model agreement for formal outputs.** The closest prior work uses cross-model agreement for formal languages. Bayless et al. [17] check NL-to-SMT translations from multiple LLMs, scoring each by the fraction of peers whose output entails it (the same score form as our consensus metric), but they evaluate on a fixed schema with downstream QA labels rather than per-candidate faithfulness. Alvanaki et al. [18] apply cross-model formal consensus to RTL (hardware description language), reporting precision at coverage thresholds for different numbers of agreeing models. Singh et al. [19] train a generative verifier for NL-to-FOL autoformalization, achieving AUROC 0.961 on Z3-reference labels; however, this verifier degrades when labels switch from solver equivalence to human intent. Wang et al. [20] apply selective conformal prediction with self-consistency to NL-to-temporal-logic, finding that self-consistency AUROC rises with problem difficulty. None of these works reports a meta-evaluation of cross-family consensus as a per-candidate NL-to-FOL faithfulness score against an LLM judge, nested over the baseline stack.", " ", "-**Round-trip and self-consistency.** Amrollahi et al. [7] propose verbalising formal statements back to natural language and checking consistency, with high accuracy on mathematical autoformalization. Our round-trip baseline follows the same pattern but achieves only AUROC 0.710 on NL-to-FOL. Self-consistency [8] scores a candidate by agreement with other samples from the same model. In our setting, cross-family consensus outperforms single-model self-consistency by +0.140 [0.085, 0.197] (Section 5), because self-consistency conflates model-specific biases with genuine correctness. Kuhn et al. [12] formalise semantic uncertainty via equivalence classes; our consensus score is structurally similar but uses z3 equivalence across families rather than meaning equivalence within a single model.", "+**Correlated failures in multi-version systems.** Eckhardt and Lee [21] showed theoretically that coincident failures in independently developed software versions need not be independent; empirical studies confirmed that correlated errors are common. Parse-based metrics verify only that the output is syntactically valid FOL [6, 7], which is necessary but far from sufficient. None of these works reports a per-candidate NL-to-FOL faithfulness meta-evaluation of cross-family consensus against an LLM judge baseline, nested over the baseline stack.\n\n**Correlated failures in multi-version systems.** Eckhardt and Lee [21] showed theoretically that coincident failures in independently developed software versions need not be independent; empirical studies confirmed that correlated errors are common. Our scatter analysis (Section 5) echoes this finding: errors produced by different LLM families are correlated but far less so than correct translations, providing the asymmetry that consensus exploits.\n\n## 3 Method\n\n### 3.1 Cross-Family Solver Consensus\n\nGiven a natural-language sentence $s$ and a candidate FOL formula $c$ produced by any system, the consensus metric proceeds in three steps.\n\n**Step 1: Peer generation.** Collect translations of $s$ from $k$ LLM families, each family producing one translation at temperature 0 with a standardised few-shot prompt. The families must be architecturally independent (different pre-training data, different organisations). In our experiments we use nine families spanning six organisations.\n\n**Step 2: Pairwise equivalence.** For each peer translation $p_i$, check Z3 equivalence between $c$ and $p_i$ modulo vocabulary alignment. The vocabulary aligner maps predicate names in $p_i$ to those in $c$ by string similarity (normalised Levenshtein distance on lowercased names with matching arity), then checks Z3 equivalence under the best injective mapping. Two formulas are equivalent modulo vocabulary (eqmv) when there exists an injective, arity-preserving symbol map under which Z3 confirms logical equivalence.\n\n**Step 3: Consensus score.** The consensus score is:\n\n$$\\text{c\\_score} = 1 - \\frac{1}{k}\\sum_{i=1}^{k} \\mathbf{1}[\\text{eqmv}(c, p_i)]$$\n\nwhere eqmv denotes equivalence modulo vocabulary. Higher scores indicate greater disagreement with the peer pool, predicting error. The candidate itself is excluded from the pool (leave-one-out when the candidate is one of the generated translations).\n\n[FIGURE:fig_method]\n\n### 3.2 Graded versus Binary Consensus\n\nRather than binary majority voting, we use the graded consensus score, which preserves the continuous fraction of disagreeing peers. On the held-out test set, graded consensus outperforms binary majority voting by a stratified AUROC margin of +0.114 [0.091, 0.140] [ARTIFACT:gen_art_evaluation_2], because partial agreement carries information that a binary threshold discards. Error endorsement (the rate at which the majority endorses an erroneous candidate, e = 0.124) and correct-candidate divergence (the rate at which a correct candidate disagrees with the majority, d = 0.537) are both substantial, so the graded score discriminates where the binary vote does not.\n\n### 3.3 Text-Augmented Fusion\n\nTo complement the consensus signal with text-level checks, we define a fused metric (PEER+TEXT) that combines the consensus score with two text-only features: (i) a bag-of-words coverage score measuring overlap between text content words and formula predicates, and (ii) a role-questionnaire score in which a small LLM answers structured questions about the sentence while Z3 extracts the formula's role profile, and their answers are compared [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_1]. The fusion weights are fitted by logistic regression on a development screen and frozen before the held-out evaluation.\n\n## 4 Experimental Setup\n\n### 4.1 Development Screen\n\nThe development screen uses Logic-LM [1] released outputs on FOLIO validation: three LLM systems (GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4, text-davinci-003) producing 796 items on the validation split. Labels are assigned by Z3 equivalence to corrected gold formulas [5]. After filtering to parseable and labelled items, the primary population contains 546 items (249 ERROR, 297 CORRECT). The screen is dominated by short sentences (93% under 12 words). [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_3] [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_4]\n\n### 4.2 Held-Out Test Set\n\nThe held-out test set contains 8,507 real NL-to-FOL candidates for 700 sentences drawn from FOLIO training premises and MALLS training data, with strata enriched for long sentences (25+ words, 3+ conditions) and exception clauses [ARTIFACT:gen_art_dataset_1]. Ten generator slots across nine LLM families produce candidates at temperature 0 with few-shot prompts. Labels combine Z3 equivalence to audited gold references with a blind, nonce-disguised (content words replaced by nonsense tokens to prevent memorisation), family-disjoint adjudication panel (Claude Haiku-4.5, GLM-4.6, Kimi-K2). Tier A labels come from Z3 equivalence alone; tier B labels are resolved by the panel for cases involving vocabulary granularity or compound differences. The primary analysis population (tiers A+B) contains 2,686 scorable items (1,822 ERROR, 864 CORRECT) across 292 sentences. All bootstraps cluster by sentence to account for within-sentence dependence (B = 2,000).\n\n### 4.3 Perturbation Suite\n\nA suite of 4,234 typed mutants and 868 meaning-preserving controls was constructed from 300 base formulas with trusted references [ARTIFACT:gen_art_dataset_3]. Mutant operators include NEG (negation flip), REV (argument reversal), QUANT (quantifier change), RESTR (restriction change), CONN (connective change), MOVE (scope movement), DROP (dropped condition), ADD (added condition), SWAP (argument swap), BIND (binding change), and MEANING_RENAME (semantically different predicate name). Controls include synonym renaming, nonce renaming, reordering, contrapositive, and De Morgan rewrites. Each mutant is Z3-verified as non-equivalent to its base; each control is Z3-verified as equivalent. This suite enables within-base sensitivity analysis: for each base formula, compare the metric's ability to distinguish its mutants from its controls.\n\n### 4.4 Long-Sentence Test Set\n\nThe long-sentence test set contains 221 templated sentences, each at least 25 words long with at least three conditions and one unless/except/provided-that/only-if clause, with references trusted by construction from a verified atom lexicon [ARTIFACT:gen_art_dataset_3]. In the shared-vocabulary (SIG) condition, generators receive the sentence plus the reference's symbol list; labels are pure Z3 equivalence to the reference. This condition isolates consensus's discriminative power when vocabulary variation is removed.\n\n### 4.5 Baselines\n\nWe compare consensus against:\n\n- **LLM judge**: Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite with a rubric-based JSON scoring prompt, run on both nonce-disguised and original text views. [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_4] [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_6]\n- **Frontier judge**: Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview, original text view. [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_6]\n- **Self-consistency** (SC-5): five samples from GPT-4.1-Nano at temperature 0.7, scored by Z3 equivalence fraction. [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_3]\n- **Round-trip NLI**: verbalise the formula back to natural language, compare to the original sentence via bidirectional NLI entailment. [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_4]\n- **Baseline stack** (S4): cross-fitted logistic regression combining all cheap baselines (judges, round-trip, structural features). [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_6]\n- **Structural pilot metrics**: parse rate, joint conflict, arity inconsistency, predicate-set overlap, dangling predicates. [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_4]\n\n### 4.6 Pre-Registration\n\nThe held-out evaluation was pre-registered before any score on the held-out test set was computed. The pre-registration specifies the primary population (tiers A+B), the stratified bootstrap procedure (B = 2,000, clustered by sentence), and the confirmatory criterion: the 95% CI of the stratified AUROC difference between consensus and the disguised cheap judge must exclude zero. [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_6]\n\n## 5 Results\n\n### 5.1 Main Results\n\nTable 1 presents the pre-registered held-out results on the primary population (2,686 items, 1,822 ERROR, 864 CORRECT, 292 sentences).\n\n| Metric | Strat. AUROC | Pooled AUROC | 95% CI (strat.) |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Cross-family consensus | 0.741 | 0.782 | [0.708, 0.773] |\n| PEER+TEXT fusion | 0.753 | 0.790 | [0.714, 0.788] |\n| Disguised cheap judge | 0.642 | 0.696 | [0.598, 0.687] |\n| Original cheap judge | 0.623 | 0.635 | [0.575, 0.670] |\n| Best cheap judge (nano) | 0.652 | -- | -- |\n| Baseline stack (S4) | 0.704 | 0.759 | -- |\n| Local 8B judge (disguised) | 0.669 | 0.712 | -- |\n\n[ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_6]\n\n**Headline result.** Consensus outperforms the disguised cheap judge by a stratified AUROC difference of +0.099 [0.049, 0.146] (pre-registered and confirmed; p < 0.001 by one-sided bootstrap). [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_6] On the long-sentence pool (2,300 items from the L25, L20, and EXC strata), the advantage widens to +0.116 [0.070, 0.163]. On the L20+EXC subset with tier-A labels (449 items where the gold reference is fully trusted), the advantage is +0.299 [0.212, 0.390].\n\n**Nested gain over the baseline stack.** Consensus adds information beyond all cheap baselines combined: the nested AUROC gain of adding consensus to the baseline stack is +0.039 [0.021, 0.057] (stratified), with a permutation-null 95th percentile of 0.009. Consensus alone approximately equals the full baseline stack (+0.006 [-0.031, 0.042]). [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_6]\n\n**Frontier judge comparison.** On the 284-row frontier-judge subsample, consensus achieves an AUROC ratio of 0.957 [0.887, 1.034] relative to the frontier judge (Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview), at 30x lower cost per item ($0.00012 vs $0.00365). Adding consensus to the frontier judge raises its AUROC by +0.037 [0.008, 0.066]. [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_6]\n\n[FIGURE:fig_main_results]\n\n### 5.2 Long Sentences with Shared Vocabulary\n\nOn the long-sentence test set in the shared-vocabulary condition (1,904 candidates from 220 sentences, 395 ERROR, 1,509 CORRECT), consensus achieves within-template AUROC 0.954 [0.939, 0.968] versus the disguised judge at 0.587 [0.551, 0.622], a confirmed delta of +0.367 [0.328, 0.404] [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_7]. The judge adds nothing over consensus in this condition: the nested gain of adding the judge to consensus is approximately zero, while adding consensus to the judge gives +0.377.\n\nOn a 60-row frontier subsample from the same test set, consensus achieves 0.956 versus the frontier judge at 0.932 (original text) and 0.735 (disguised). When vocabulary is controlled, consensus matches the frontier judge.\n\n### 5.3 Perturbation Sensitivity\n\nOn the perturbation suite (4,234 mutants + 868 controls, within-base design), consensus achieves within-base AUROC 0.866, compared to 0.680 for the disguised judge, 0.666 for self-consistency, 0.659 for bag-of-words coverage, and approximately 0.50 for the structural pilot metrics [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_8]. The PEER+TEXT fusion reaches 0.948. Consensus detects DOWN-polarity and UP-polarity edits symmetrically (difference < 0.01 AUROC), while local judges and embedding-based round-trip miss DOWN-polarity edits by 0.12 to 0.15 AUROC.\n\n[FIGURE:fig_perturb]\n\n### 5.4 How Many Peer Families Are Needed?\n\nThe discriminative power of consensus saturates rapidly. On the held-out test set (2,014 items with all seven non-candidate families available), pooled AUROC rises from 0.685 (one family) through 0.757 (three families) to 0.784 (seven families) [ARTIFACT:gen_art_evaluation_2]. Three families capture 97% of the full pool's AUROC. The cross-fitted best three-family pool (DeepSeek, Microsoft, OpenAI) achieves 0.785, matching the full pool. No single family carries the signal: the maximum leave-one-family-out AUROC drop is 0.005.\n\n[FIGURE:fig_kcurve]\n\n### 5.5 Why Consensus Discriminates\n\nThe consensus metric works because correct and erroneous translations exhibit different agreement patterns. On the held-out test set, the mean pairwise agreement rate among translations of the same sentence is 0.760 for correct candidates and 0.159 for erroneous ones (a scatter ratio of 4.8) [ARTIFACT:gen_art_evaluation_2]. Correct translations converge on the same logical content despite different surface forms, while errors are structurally diverse: different families produce different wrong formulas for the same sentence.\n\nThe graded consensus score outperforms binary majority voting by +0.114 [0.091, 0.140] stratified AUROC. Binary voting collapses the continuous agreement fraction into a single bit, losing discriminative information when error endorsement (e = 0.124) and correct-candidate divergence (d = 0.537) are both far from zero. [ARTIFACT:gen_art_evaluation_2]\n\n### 5.6 Development-Screen Results\n\nOn the development screen (546 items, 249 ERROR, 297 CORRECT), consensus achieves AUROC 0.866 [0.821, 0.906] versus self-consistency at 0.725 [0.669, 0.781], a paired delta of +0.140 [0.085, 0.197] [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_3]. On a vocabulary-controlled subset (82 errors remaining after removing items where the aligner confound determines the label), consensus achieves 0.852 versus self-consistency at 0.714. The development-screen AUROC (0.866) is higher than the held-out pooled AUROC (0.782), reflecting the screen's simpler, shorter sentences.\n\n### 5.7 Negative Results\n\n**Structural pilot metrics.** The user's pilot structural metrics (joint conflict, arity inconsistency, shape inconsistency, dangling predicates) achieve AUROC 0.500 to 0.533 on the development screen, indistinguishable from chance [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_4]. Only the cross-system predicate-set Jaccard (0.720) carries signal, and it is a coarser proxy for the consensus approach.\n\n**Formula lint.** Deterministic formula-smell detection achieves AUROC 0.508 on LLM outputs, a negative result: lint rules that fire on human annotation errors (AUROC 0.655) do not transfer to LLM outputs, which produce semantic rather than syntactic errors [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_1].\n\n**Round-trip reformalisation.** Verbalising the formula and re-translating to FOL to check Z3 equivalence achieves AUROC 0.513, near chance, because 76% of items produce tied scores [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_4].\n\n**Candidate-signature consensus.** Giving peers the candidate's own symbol list, rather than letting them choose their own vocabulary, was intended to reduce correct-candidate divergence. It does lower divergence (d = 0.139 vs 0.323 for free peers) but raises error endorsement (e = 0.459 vs 0.173), producing a net AUROC of 0.614 versus 0.770 for free peers [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_9]. Anchoring the peers to the candidate's vocabulary causes them to reproduce its errors.\n\n## 6 Discussion and Limitations\n\n### 6.1 Vocabulary Dependence\n\nThe principal limitation of consensus is vocabulary dependence. Two formulas with different predicate names are not Z3-equivalent under any identity map, so a candidate using a synonym or a different decomposition than its peers is penalised regardless of correctness. On the perturbation suite, the nonce-rename false-alarm rate is 0.76 [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_8]. We tested three approaches to vocabulary-robust equivalence: name-free alignment (exhaustive injective symbol mapping without string similarity), hybrid matching (combining name-based and name-free maps), and gloss-gated checking (verifying renamed pairs with an LLM gloss). All three reduce correct-candidate divergence but proportionally increase error endorsement, producing no net AUROC gain [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_14]. The gloss-gated checker failed its development gate (all-stratum AUROC 0.696 vs 0.742 for plain vocabulary alignment). This tradeoff between divergence and endorsement appears structural when vocabulary is unconstrained.\n\nIn practice, vocabulary dependence is mitigated by standardising the symbol vocabulary in the generation prompt (as in the shared-vocabulary condition, where consensus reaches AUROC 0.954) or by pairing consensus with a vocabulary-independent text-level check.\n\n### 6.2 Error Endorsement\n\nConsensus cannot detect errors that all peers reproduce. On the held-out test set, 38% of errors are endorsed by the majority. The endorsed-error rate is higher for structural errors (57%) than for polarity errors (5%). Text-level checks detect some endorsed errors that consensus misses, but the PEER+TEXT fusion does not significantly outperform consensus alone on the held-out test (stratified delta +0.011, not significant) [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_5].\n\n### 6.3 Contamination and Judge Comparison\n\nThe disguised-judge comparison controls for LLM memorisation of public benchmark data by replacing content words with nonsense tokens. The flash-lite contamination difference-in-differences on the held-out test set is +0.105 [0.006, 0.201], suggesting a small memorisation benefit for the judge on some items [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_6]. Consensus, which uses only Z3 equivalence, is structurally immune to memorisation.\n\nOn the development screen, judges are highly sensitive to meaning-preserving rewrites: the verdict flip rate under contrapositive rewriting is 0.41 to 0.95 for judges versus 0.0 for consensus [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_4]. Consensus is invariant to any rewrite that preserves Z3 equivalence, but not to vocabulary changes.\n\n### 6.4 Short-Sentence Weakness\n\nThe consensus advantage over the judge does not hold on short FOLIO-style sentences (CTRL stratum: -0.069 [-0.23, 0.10]) [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_6]. The method is strongest on long, conditioned sentences where judges struggle with the logical complexity.\n\n### 6.5 Label Protocol Sensitivity\n\nConsensus's AUROC depends on the label protocol. Under solver-only labels (development screen), consensus achieves 0.866; under panel-adjudicated labels (held-out test, tiers A+B), the stratified AUROC is 0.741 [ARTIFACT:gen_art_evaluation_1]. Part of this drop is explained by the panel's stricter standard: it accepts only 61% of expert-corrected formulas. Another part reflects instrument confounding: consensus and the solver labeller share the vocabulary aligner, which inflates consensus's score on items where vocabulary alignment determines the label.\n\n### 6.6 Incomplete Confirmations\n\nConfirmation was attempted on three additional fronts: a fresh 550-sentence test set, a second long-sentence sample, and the long-sentence test set under free vocabulary (no shared symbol list). All three were budget-stopped before reaching testability [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_11] [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_12] [ARTIFACT:gen_art_experiment_13]. The only fully confirmed results are on the held-out test set (developed during the same run but scored once after pre-registration) and the long-sentence test set under shared vocabulary (templated sentences).\n\n## 7 Conclusion\n\nCross-family solver consensus is a practical gold-free faithfulness metric for NL-to-FOL translation. On a pre-registered held-out test, it outperforms the best cheap LLM judge by +0.099 [0.049, 0.146] stratified AUROC, and on long sentences with controlled vocabulary it reaches 0.954. The method costs under $0.001 per candidate with three peer families, is domain-agnostic, and is structurally immune to memorisation. Its vocabulary dependence is the central unsolved problem: when candidate and peers use different predicate names, consensus penalises correct translations and endorses vocabulary-matched errors. Standardising the symbol vocabulary in generation prompts removes this limitation. Future work should develop vocabulary-robust equivalence checks that do not trade divergence for endorsement, and extend the evaluation to richer formal languages where solver-based equivalence remains tractable.\n\n## References\n\n[1] L. The translation step is hard to evaluate. A correct formalisation of a sentence is not unique: different predicate names, different decompositions of the same concept, and logically equivalent rewrites can all be faithful. Gold FOL annotations are expensive and unreliable: recent audits found that roughly 40% of entries in both FOLIO [3] and MALLS [4] contain errors [5]. The metrics in common use either require a gold formula (exact match, BLEU, prover-checked equivalence) or only verify that the output parses [6, 7]. Structural consistency checks, such as arity agreement, predicate-set overlap across reruns, and joint satisfiability, measure stability and composability but not whether a formula says what its sentence says [8].\\n\\nThis gap matters in practice. As NL-to-FOL pipelines are deployed for contract analysis, requirement verification, and knowledge-base construction, practitioners need a metric that predicts faithfulness at scale, without gold formulas, and cheaply enough to run on every output.\\n\\nWe observe that when multiple independent LLM families translate the same sentence, their translations tend to agree (in the sense of Z3 equivalence) when they are correct and to scatter when at least one is wrong. This asymmetry motivates cross-family solver consensus: score each candidate by the fraction of independently generated peer translations that are Z3-equivalent to it, after vocabulary alignment. A candidate that most peers agree with is likely faithful; one that no peer reproduces is likely erroneous.\\n\\nThis paper makes the following contributions:\\n\\n- We define cross-family solver consensus, a gold-free, domain-agnostic faithfulness metric for NL-to-FOL that requires only a sentence and a set of peer translations. On a pre-registered held-out test (2,686 candidates, 292 sentences), consensus achieves stratified AUROC 0.741 versus 0.642 for the best cheap LLM judge, a confirmed advantage of +0.099 [0.049, 0.146] (Section 5). Section 5 reports results. Section 6 discusses findings and limitations. Section 7 concludes.\\n\\n[FIGURE:fig1]\\n\\n## 2 Related Work\\n\\n**NL-to-FOL evaluation metrics.** Existing faithfulness metrics for NL-to-FOL fall into three categories. Gold-based metrics check equivalence to a reference formula, either syntactically (exact match, tree edit distance) or semantically (prover-checked logical equivalence) [6, 8]. They require a gold formula and fail silently when the gold is wrong. Thatikonda et al. [8] evaluate several FOL closeness metrics and find that they correlate poorly with human judgements of faithfulness. Parse-based metrics verify only that the output is syntactically valid FOL [6, 7], which is necessary but far from sufficient. LLM-as-judge approaches prompt a language model to compare the candidate to the source text [9]; they are flexible but expensive per item and sensitive to meaning-preserving rewrites of the formula.\\n\\n**Self-consistency and sampling agreement.** Self-consistency [10] scores a candidate by agreement among multiple samples from the same model. In NL-to-code, minimum Bayes risk decoding uses execution-based agreement among samples to select outputs [11, 12, 13]. SAC3 [14] extends self-consistency across models for hallucination detection. Semantic entropy [15, 16] clusters sampled outputs by semantic equivalence and measures the entropy of the cluster distribution. These methods use a single model's samples or ad hoc similarity; they do not exploit the formal semantics of FOL (Z3 equivalence) or require family diversity.\\n\\n**Cross-model agreement for formal outputs.** The closest prior work uses cross-model agreement for formal languages. Bayless et al. [17] translate natural language into SMT-LIB from multiple LLMs and score each translation by the fraction of peers whose output entails it, the same score form as our consensus metric, but they evaluate on a fixed schema with downstream QA labels rather than per-candidate faithfulness meta-evaluation. Alvanaki et al. [18] apply cross-model formal consensus to RTL (hardware description language), reporting that precision rises from 63% to 95% as the required number of agreeing models increases from one to four, but they measure coverage rather than per-candidate AUROC. Singh et al. [19] train a generative verifier for mathematical autoformalization, achieving AUROC 0.961 on Z3-reference labels; however, this verifier degrades when labels switch from solver equivalence to human intent. Wang et al. [20] apply selective conformal prediction with self-consistency to NL-to-temporal-logic, finding that self-consistency AUROC rises with problem difficulty. None of these works reports a per-candidate NL-to-FOL faithfulness meta-evaluation of cross-family consensus against an LLM judge baseline, nested over the baseline stack.\\n\\n**Correlated failures in multi-version systems.** Eckhardt and Lee [21] showed theoretically that coincident failures in independently developed software versions need not be independent; empirical studies confirmed that correlated errors are common. Our scatter analysis (Section 5) echoes this finding: errors produced by different LLM families are correlated but far less so than correct translations, providing the asymmetry that consensus exploits.\\n\\n## 3 Method\\n\\n### 3.1 Cross-Family Solver Consensus\\n\\nGiven a natural-language sentence $s$ and a candidate FOL formula $c$ produced by any system, the consensus metric proceeds in three steps.\\n\\n**Step 1: Peer generation.** Collect translations of $s$ from $k$ LLM families, each family producing one translation at temperature 0 with a standardised few-shot prompt. The families must be architecturally independent (different pre-training data, different organisations). In our experiments we use nine families spanning six organisations.\\n\\n**Step 2: Pairwise equivalence.** For each peer translation $p_i$, check Z3 equivalence between $c$ and $p_i$ modulo vocabulary alignment. The vocabulary aligner maps predicate names in $p_i$ to those in $c$ by string similarity (normalised Levenshtein distance on lowercased names with matching arity), then checks Z3 equivalence under the best injective mapping. Two formulas are equivalent modulo vocabulary (eqmv) when there exists an injective, arity-preserving symbol map under which Z3 confirms logical equivalence.\\n\\n**Step 3: Consensus score.** The consensus score is:\\n\\n$$\\\\text{c\\\\_score} = 1 - \\\\frac{1}{k}\\\\sum_{i=1}^{k} \\\\mathbf{1}[\\\\text{eqmv}(c, p_i)]$$\\n\\nwhere eqmv denotes equivalence modulo vocabulary. The translation step is hard to evaluate. A correct formalisation of a sentence is not unique: different predicate names, different decompositions of the same concept, and logically equivalent rewrites can all be faithful. Gold FOL annotations are expensive and unreliable: recent audits found that roughly 40% of entries in both FOLIO [3] and MALLS [4] contain errors [5].
